messages.subject: rgl snapshot
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have used the function 'plotReftoTarget' to make nice figures of my extreme shapes compared with the calculated mean shape (calculated from the data with the function 'mshape). For my 2D data, saving the figures works fine because they open as a 'regular' R figure and can be exported as PDF.

For my 3D data however, a rgl window opens. After rotating the object to get the best possible side, I try exporting the figure as pdf using the function 'rgl.postscript' (described by the rgl documentation as the way to export an rgl window). However, the quality of the figure is really low compared with the quality of the figure when still in the rgl window (I added one as an example). I also tried taking a printscreen, but the quality of the figure is just as poor, and I want to be able to edit the figure afterwards using Adobe Illustrator etc.

I was wondering whether anyone has come across this problem and has managed to fix it? I feel that there must be a solution that I'm overlooking. There must be a way to export these nice 3D images to a pdf to be implemented in a paper!

Thanks in advance!

Sara

S.J. van de Kerke | PhD candidate

Wageningen University | Biosystematics Group

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Question about surface alignment
messages.body_plain:
Tim,

You might consider first trying the analysis with procD = TRUE, just to see what happens.  I am not advocating this as a solution, but if it seems to produce a more reasonable outcome, you might identify the problem is due to semilandmark density.

I have found that using a bending energy approach to sliders when the density of semilandmarks is high can cause this problem but using a minimized Procrustes approach does not, as it becomes essentially the same as treating the semilandmarks as fixed when there are so many.  In such cases, it might be just that the density of surface points is too extreme to try to use bending energy (presumably because the PC tangent plane used is ill-defined if points are not spread out a bit).

I prefer using bending energy compared to minimized Procrustes distance, but at some point, trying to slide semilandmarks that are so adjacent to each other becomes an unnecessary step.

I hope that makes sense.

Cheers!
Mike

For some reason it totally distores two out of eight curves (with 5-10 semiLM each) in one of my sampled species (n=5), creating a loop (see figure "Distortion.tif", black:mean, red:target specimen), while all other specimen (n=107) are fine (figure Otherspecies.tif). Hence, semiLM are more anteriorly shifted on the mouth outline and this seems to affect also the sliding of the other curves within the cranium for some reason.

Best,
Peter

messages.subject_clean: Integration in the context of environmental variation
messages.body_plain:
Hi all

I’m examining the influence of environmental variables on hind leg weapon variation in male monkey beetles. I have specimens and environmental data from nine sites, and I’m interested in looking at whether differences in weapon form between sites align with differences in habitat variables (e.g. size of the flowers that the beetles fight on) between those sites.

I’ve captured landmarks for the femurs, tibias, tarsae and tarsal claws in separate files and have so far analysed patterns of shape and size variation for each of these leg segments separately, using mixed models in R with the lme() function. But in the real world, these different leg components are of course interacting and being used in combination with one another in males’ battles. I want to be able to assess whether they exhibit modularity and if so, covariation with one another. I have used geomorph’s integration.test and modularity.test functions to do so, and there does seem to be a case for each leg component to function as a module that exhibits integration with the other leg component modules (to a greater or lesser extent) (see sample plot below). What would really tie in nicely with the rest of the story, however, would be if it were possible to assess whether leg components are more or less integrated depending on differences in environmental variables between the sites in which specimens were collected from. I.e. is there a correlation between environment and morphometric integration? The thinking behind this is that the beetles live, feed and fight on asteraceae and aizoaceae flowers – both disc-shaped – that provide a fighting arena. Arena size as well as other-site specific variables may influence optimal fighting style, which in turn may select for different types of hind leg component ‘elaboration’ in different populations.

I do have phylogenetic data that is in preparation and am keen to explore modularity and integration in a phylogenetic context once that data is ready.

Thanks in advance!

Kind regards

Ariella

messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] test for variance inflation factors or not?
messages.body_plain:
Jessica,

That does not mean the same thing.  The QR decomposition warning is because one has a model design matrix, X, that has rank lower than the number of columns in X.  This is caused by the same variable more than once in the matrix, which most frequently occurs because of vectors of 0s.  The cause of vectors of 0s is most often missing interactions.  For example, if one has populations A, B, and C nested in species 1 and D and E in species 2, the species1:D, species1:E, species2:A, species2:B, and species2:C terms in the model design - columns in the design matrix - are all vectors of 0s.  These are removed via QR decomposition and the warning message is just to let you know it happened.  These columns of 0s will not be counted toward degrees of freedom and removing them will help to make sure there are no computation errors in calculating linear model coefficients.

If this is what you meant by collinear factors, then yes, it was adjusted naturally by the analysis.

Cheers!
Mike

No, this is not part of the morphol.disaprity output.  morphol.disparity performs hypothesis tests on variances, which are based on squared distances, and therefore, seem connected.  However, distances are calculated more directly from residuals, which are linear model output, meaning procD.lm is the best way to get that information.

Mike
